Preview text: The difference is in method — the facts the copy is allowed to claim, then a cold read of every draft.

Your account is already open. Signing in puts you in a workspace where you register your brand, add the real material for one launch or onboarding offer, and ask for the emails you need in your own words.

MarketingOS hands back reviewed draft text — subject, preview, body, call to action — for you to check and copy into whatever you send with. It drafts; it does not send.

Five onboarding emails out of a chat model in an afternoon is a fair comparison to make. The difference is in method, not in adjectives.

Your material is read into a set of facts the writing is allowed to claim, so each sentence traces back to something you supplied.

None of it exists until the setup is done: a new account has no campaign waiting, so the brand and the real material go in first, then one request.

Sign in to your workspace → https://app.orqagent.com/login/

- MarketingOS, private pilot

assets.content:
Subject: The quote behind every fact it claims
Preview text: Plus the cold read: what that reader understood, where it stopped, and the doubt it named.

Hi {{first_name}},

A draft either claims something your own material supports, or it does not. That is checkable rather than arguable.

MarketingOS drafts launch and onboarding email copy from whatever you point it at — a URL, a PDF, a screenshot, pasted text — and shows the source quote behind each fact it was allowed to use.

On a finished run, the Knowledge page lists those compiled facts beside the quotation each one came from, with a strength label and the gaps it could not fill.

The execution page holds the draft and its cold read: what an AI reader given no brief took the offer to be, where it stopped, the doubt it named, the changes it suggested. Not opens or clicks — a critique you can argue with.

You are the last check on facts, links and brand voice, so your edit is the measurement the pilot wants: which lines you keep, which you rewrite, what came back wrong, how long it took. Nothing to write up afterwards that the check itself does not produce.

Signing in opens your workspace rather than a draft. Both pages belong to a run — read them on one that has finished, or one real offer and one request starts one.

Sign in to check a run → https://app.orqagent.com/login/

- MarketingOS, private pilot

P.S. A run takes several minutes and can come back asking for more material; the two pages are waiting on it once it finishes.

report.request: Write exactly two English emails introducing MarketingOS to invited early-access testers who already have a test account. They run a small SaaS business and need to write a launch or onboarding email campaign. Explain one concrete supported reason to try the product, then invite them to test one real offer and review the output. Do not assume their present tools, revenue, list size, staffing, email results or urgency. Do not invent prices, testimonials, performance gains or public signup. Make the first action small: sign in, add the real offer material, and request one email. In the second email explain why inspecting source facts and reader feedback is useful. One clear CTA in each email to their existing account. The product is MarketingOS, not the older orqAgent AI agent builder.

What the email adds on its own: that I'd otherwise be getting 'five onboarding emails out of a chat model in an afternoon' (email-only — nothing in my profile says what I currently use, or that I've tried a chat model for this), that I have the 'real material' for an offer already assembled in a form I can paste (email-only, plausible but unverified), and that editing time and factual errors are a pain I've measured (email-only — the P.S. asks for them, which is fair as a pilot ask, but it presumes a baseline I haven't reported). 'Not opens or clicks — a critique you can argue with' assumes I was expecting opens and clicks — I wasn't; drop the contrast or name what the critique looks like (one example line of a doubt it named).

'so your edit is the measurement the pilot wants: which lines you keep, which you rewrite, what came back wrong, how long it took' — this is four asks dressed as one; say the one thing you actually need back.
The P.S. ('A run takes several minutes and can come back asking for more material') is the real cost and it's buried last; put the time cost next to the CTA so I can decide in one pass.
reader_verdicts.persona:
Selected audience (user-stated constraints): Invited early-access testers with an existing account who operate a small SaaS business and need launch or onboarding email copy..
Only these audience facts are established. Do not substitute a compiled market segment, invent an installed tool or experience, or infer the campaign's desired reaction. Read the email cold as this person.
Reading emphasis: weigh the effort of the next step against its usefulness. Do not assume an installed tool, a switching project or an existing workflow beyond the profile.

reader_verdicts.what_it_sells: Software that writes launch and onboarding email copy from material I point it at (URL, PDF, screenshot, pasted text), shows the exact source quote behind every fact it used plus what it couldn't source, and gives the draft a no-brief AI 'cold read' critique — so my week changes by me editing a sourced draft instead of writing from scratch and fact-checking myself.
reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: Profile-supported: I am an invited early-access tester with an existing account, I run a small SaaS, and I need launch/onboarding email copy. The email's core premise — a pilot run that drafts exactly that kind of copy and asks for my edit — lines up with all three, and the sign-off ('MarketingOS, private pilot') matches a relationship I actually have, so this does not read cold. Email-only: that I have material worth pointing it at (a page, a PDF, a deck) and an offer currently in flight; plausible for a small SaaS but not established here. Email-only and weaker: that unsourced or wrongly-sourced claims are a problem I have been having, and that I have a draft-review habit to compare against — neither is in my profile. Unknowns the copy leaves open: how long my own editing pass takes, what the minimum input is, whether anything exists in my workspace already, and whether the output is close enough to ship or close enough only to critique. Those are doubts about the ask, not a mismatch of situation.
assumed_experiences: That I need launch or onboarding email copy — profile-supported
That I have an existing account I can sign into for a private pilot — profile-supported
That I have source material (URL, PDF, screenshot, pasted text) describing a real offer to point it at — email-only, plausible but unstated
That I have a 'real offer' live or imminent that needs copy right now — email-only
That fact-checking claims against my own material is currently a chore or a failure point for me — email-only, not established
That I already know what a 'run', the 'Knowledge page' and the 'execution page' are — email-only; the terms are explained adequately but assume familiarity with the workspace layout
That I care about critique over opens/clicks as the measurement — email-only inference about my preferences
reader_verdicts.problem_now: Needing launch/onboarding copy is documented as my situation, so the subject matter is live. Whether it is urgent this Tuesday is unknown — nothing in my profile sets a launch date, and the email wisely doesn't claim one. The specific pain it leans on (claims not traceable to my own material) is a plausible risk for me rather than a documented incident; I have not reported being burned by an invented fact. The real present constraint is time: I am three minutes from a meeting and the ask is a multi-minute run plus my editing pass.
reader_verdicts.stopped_at: Both pages belong to a run — read them on one that has finished, or one real offer and one request starts one.
reader_verdicts.biggest_doubt: Effort and timing against unknown payoff. The honest cost is not 'sign in' — it is find the right source material, wait several minutes, possibly get asked for more material, then read two pages and do a full edit pass so my edit can be 'the measurement the pilot wants'. Nothing here tells me how long my part takes or how close the draft lands, and the cold read being another AI judging the first AI doesn't tell me whether the facts came back right. I am happy to try a run; I am not ready to commit a morning to being the pilot's measurement instrument.
reader_verdicts.to_click_it_would_have_to: I would have clicked if this email had told me the smallest possible first step with its real cost in it — e.g. 'paste one pricing-page URL, the run takes about six minutes, you get a sourced onboarding email and five quote-to-fact pairs to check' — or shown me one actual fact next to its actual quote so I could judge the output without starting anything.
fixes: Cut or rewrite: 'Both pages belong to a run — read them on one that has finished, or one real offer and one request starts one.' I read this twice and still had to reverse-engineer it. Say plainly: 'If a run has already finished, open it. If not, one offer plus one request starts one.'

Rewrite the subject: 'The quote behind every fact it claims' never says who is writing and never names the product. For a pilot I'm already in, 'MarketingOS: see the quote behind every fact in your draft' earns the open on recognition instead of riddle.

Rewrite: 'You are the last check on facts, links and brand voice, so your edit is the measurement the pilot wants: which lines you keep, which you rewrite, what came back wrong, how long it took.' This reads as an assignment with homework attached. Tell me what I get first; ask for the edit log second, and say whether it's logged automatically or I have to type it.

Fix the P.S.: 'A run takes several minutes and can come back asking for more material' is the first thing I budget against and the vaguest line in the email. Give the actual number of minutes and what 'more material' typically means.
Add one concrete artefact: a single compiled fact shown beside its source quote and its strength label. One example does more than three paragraphs describing the page.

Replace the abstract opening: 'A draft either claims something your own material supports, or it does not. That is checkable rather than arguable.' True but it spends my first line on a principle. Lead with what the product does to my inbox this week.
reader_verdicts.persona:
Selected audience (user-stated constraints): Invited early-access testers with an existing account who operate a small SaaS business and need launch or onboarding email copy..
Only these audience facts are established. Do not substitute a compiled market segment, invent an installed tool or experience, or infer the campaign's desired reaction. Read the email cold as this person.
Reading emphasis: scrutinise whether the claims earn trust for the requested next step. Do not invent a prior purchase, failed tool or bad experience; distinguish trying the product from adopting it in production.

limiting_gaps: No price or free-entry terms found - emails cannot name a price, a trial length or a risk reversal
No customer names, quotes or case studies found - the copy can describe the product but cannot prove anyone uses it
No measurable results found - claims stay qualitative, and adjectives convert worse than numbers
report.what_would_help_most: Resolve this simulated next-step obstacle: I would have clicked if this email had told me how long the setup actually takes and what exactly to bring — e.g. 'paste your pricing page and one existing welcome email, about ten minutes, first drafts back in two' — so I could judge whether it fits before the meeting or has to wait for Thursday. Check existing verified material first; surface a supported answer or documentation link appropriate to the CTA. If absent, obtain this specific information. Reader expectations are not product evidence.
report.sequence_summary: Two emails that argue one promise in the right order — earn the run, then make the run's working readable — and both stand alone; the only sequence-level slack is that email 2's reader-report half repeats email 1's claim instead of opening it the way it opens the facts page.}

brief.interpretation: Read as an activation request to people who already hold accounts, not an acquisition campaign: two emails to invited pilot users, each asking them to use the login they already have. The campaign goal is one real run on one real offer plus a review of what came back, not a purchase decision — public registration is closed and no price, trial, testimonial or result exists, so no commercial argument is available or attempted. 'Launch or onboarding email campaign' is treated as the work they already have to do (as the user stated), not as a deadline, a failing current sequence, or evidence about their tools, list, staffing or past email results — none of which are assumed anywhere in the brief. Where the request says 'one concrete supported reason', email 1 spends it on the one mechanism a prompt has no room for: material read into a fixed set of claimable facts, then every draft cold-read by a reader that never saw the brief and rewritten where it did not land. Email 2 takes the second half of the request literally: why inspecting the compiled facts and the reader report is worth the reader's time. Segment chosen is the only one whose next step actually exists; the SaaS and launch/onboarding specifics from the user's request are carried in reader_profile_override.
brief.reader:
Selected audience (user-stated constraints): Invited early-access testers with an existing account who operate a small SaaS business and need launch or onboarding email copy..
No further recipient situation is established. Compiled market context is research to check for applicability, not a replacement biography.
brief.reader_segment: An invited pilot user with a live account who still has not pushed one real offer through it
brief.reader_profile_override: Invited early-access testers with an existing account who operate a small SaaS business and need launch or onboarding email copy.
brief.promise: On one real offer, in one run, you can find out for yourself whether MarketingOS writes launch or onboarding email text you would be willing to send under your own name — and check its working rather than take its word for it.
brief.orientation: MarketingOS is what is behind the login you already have: you point it at your own offer material — your site, a PDF, a screenshot, pasted text — ask for the launch or onboarding emails you need in your own words, and it hands back reviewed draft text (subject, preview, body, call to action) for you to check and copy into whatever you send with.
brief.arc: Email 1 moves them from an unopened account to one real run: it names the one thing in the process that a blank prompt has no room for — a fixed set of claimable facts compiled from their own material, and a cold read of every draft by a reader who never saw the brief — and asks for the smallest complete action, which is sign in, register the brand, add the real offer material, request one email. Email 2 assumes the run may or may not have happened and changes what they think the output is: not a verdict to accept or reject on taste, but two inspectable pages — the compiled facts with their source quotations and strength labels, and the reader report naming what the simulated reader understood, where they stopped and their biggest doubt. Email 1 earns the run; email 2 makes the run readable, which is also what makes their pilot notes possible. Neither depends on the other being read.
brief.sequence_rationale: Two emails, and the order is forced by what exists. Nothing has been generated for this reader — a new account has no campaign waiting — so an email about how to inspect a reader report is addressed to a page they cannot open yet. Email 1 therefore has one job: make the first run exist, with the smallest action that completes (sign in, register the brand, add the real offer material, request one email) and exactly one reason to bother, chosen because it is the one thing a chat prompt structurally cannot do — fix the set of facts the writing is allowed to claim before a word is written, then have a reader who never saw the brief read the draft and rewrite what did not land. Email 2 comes second because inspection is only valuable once there is something to inspect, and because it answers the objection that email 1 deliberately leaves standing: an AI reviewing an AI proves nothing. That is answered by disclosure and a readable diagnosis, never by an implied result — so email 2 says plainly that the cold reader is a simulation and not a measurement, and argues that the critique is worth reading on its merits and the compiled facts are worth reading against their own material. Reversing the order would ask them to evaluate transparency about an output that does not exist. Both emails avoid every argument this material cannot carry: no price, no trial, no testimonial, no performance claim, no time saving (no setup time has been measured), no sector-quality claim, and no promise that the first run comes back complete. The single thing the user could send us that would most change this campaign: confirmed commercial terms — what MarketingOS costs after the pilot and whether any free entry exists — because a pilot user who likes the output currently has nothing to convert into, and that silence is the one objection neither email can answer.

emails.job: Get them to sign in, register their brand, add the real offer material for one launch or onboarding campaign, and request one email.
emails.single_idea: Before anything gets written, your material is compiled into a set of facts the writing is allowed to claim — and then every draft is read by a reader who has never seen the brief, and rewritten where it did not land; that is the part you cannot get from a blank prompt, and it only starts once you put one real offer in.
emails.felt_need: I have a launch or onboarding sequence to write and no copy for it yet, and there is an account sitting there that I have not actually used for anything.
emails.status_quo: The account is open and empty. No draft, no report, nothing generated — so the sequence is still an unstarted task, written however they would normally write it.
emails.why_it_fails: An account on its own produces nothing: a new account has no campaign waiting, and until the brand is registered and real material is in there, there is nothing to read, nothing to react to and nothing to report back.
emails.mechanism: Point it at the material you already have for this offer — your site, a PDF, a screenshot, pasted text — and ask for what you need in your own words, e.g. a five-email onboarding campaign for your SaaS. That material is read into a set of facts it is allowed to claim, so every sentence traces back to something you supplied; each draft is then read by a simulated reader who knows nothing about your product, and what did not land is rewritten before you see it. The payoff only exists after the setup step: register the brand and add the real offer material first, then request one email.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: What comes back is text, not a send: subject, preview, body and call to action, copyable or exportable with an HTML preview — nothing is sent, nothing is published, so testing it on a real offer costs you an evening, not a campaign.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: I am not handing my launch over to something that might mail my customers on my behalf, and I do not want a tool I have to migrate into.
alternative_arguments.status_quo: They write and send from whatever they already use, and keep the decision about what goes out entirely in their own hands.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: MarketingOS drafts only: the output is subject, preview, body and a call to action, with text copying or export and an HTML preview, which you review and transfer into your own sending tool. It does not send emails, publish campaigns or guarantee opens, clicks, revenue or conversions — the send stays where it is.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: trying this means letting something loose on my launch. After: trying this means asking for one draft I can read, copy or throw away, with my sending tool untouched.
must_not_say: no claim that reviewing and pasting is faster or less work than writing it — no setup or editing time has been measured
no integration or deliverability claims: nothing is established about connecting to any sending tool
do not frame the absence of sending as a competitor comparison
alternative_arguments.objection: If I still have to verify every fact and link, fix the voice and paste it into my own sender, I have not removed the work — just moved it, and I do not know whether it is less.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Sign in to your existing account, add the material for one real offer, and request one email.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether reviewed draft text in this shape — subject, preview, body, call to action — is something they would actually move into their own sending tool for this launch.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: In the workspace they can request one email against their own offer material and, when it arrives, read it as subject, preview, body and call to action, copy or export the text and preview it as HTML.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: It does not send or schedule anything, does not connect to their sending tool, and does not establish what the product costs once the pilot ends.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Promise the artefact and its boundary in plain words — draft text you can copy, nothing sent — so the open costs them no suspicion.

emails.belief_shift: Before: the account is a favour I have not got round to, and feeding a tool a thin version of my company will produce thin copy. After: the thing being tested is a specific process — fixed claimable facts, then a cold read and a rewrite — and it can only be judged by putting one real offer in, which is a half hour of material and one request.
must_not_say: no price, plan, trial length, discount or free-entry terms — none exist
no testimonials, customer names, 'other pilot users', 'companies like yours' or any implied adoption
no claim about opens, clicks, replies, revenue or conversions, and no 'better emails' performance promise
no claim that setup, material gathering or the run is quick, or takes a stated number of minutes, or saves time — no hands-on setup time has been measured
do not assume their current tools, email platform, revenue, list size, staffing, past email results or any deadline
no public signup or 'share this with a friend' — registration is closed
nothing from the older orqAgent agent builder: no Slack bot, integrations, credits or agent claims
keep the market research, audience map and LinkedIn workspace out of this email — it argues one thing
no reassurance about data storage, retention, security or confidentiality — nothing is established
do not claim the product writes well for SaaS specifically, or for any sector; sector quality is not established
do not promise the first run comes back complete
emails.objection: I could get five onboarding emails out of a chat model in an afternoon. Why does this need my evening?
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact and unhurried; a direct request from someone who knows the reader has not done it yet and is not annoyed about it.
emails.call_to_action: Sign in to the account you already have, register your brand, add the real material for one launch or onboarding offer, and request one email.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether MarketingOS produces launch or onboarding text they would be willing to send under their own name — decided on one offer that actually matters to them rather than in the abstract.
emails.next_step_value: Signing in opens their workspace, where they register the brand, add the real source material, and request one email against it; the request can be written in their own words.
emails.next_step_limit: The login opens an empty workspace, not a draft — nothing has been generated for them yet. A generation can take several minutes and may finish with partial delivery or come back asking for more material, and it does not answer what the product costs after the pilot.
emails.subject_strategy: Name the exact state of their account and the one small action that changes it. No hype adjectives, no urgency, no 'introducing' — they already know what this is, so the subject has to make the next ten minutes concrete.

emails.job: Get them to open the compiled facts and the reader report for their run — and, if they have not run one yet, to sign in and start one so there is something to read.
emails.single_idea: The useful half of a run is the working: the compiled facts with the quotation each one came from, and the report naming what the cold reader understood, where they stopped and their biggest doubt — read those and you are judging a critique you can argue with, not a score you have to trust.
emails.felt_need: I am the one whose name is on the email. If a sentence about my product is wrong, or a stranger stops reading in paragraph two, I need to see that before I send it — and an AI grading another AI's writing tells me nothing on its own.
emails.status_quo: They read a draft the way anyone reads a draft: on taste and memory, deciding sentence by sentence whether it sounds like them and whether they believe it.
emails.why_it_fails: Read on its own, a draft can only be judged by feel. It does not show you which claim came from which line of your own material, where the gaps were, or where somebody who does not already know your product lost the thread — and you are the only reader you have.
emails.mechanism: Two separate pages in the workspace carry that working. The brand's Knowledge page lists the compiled facts with the supporting source quotation, an evidence identifier, a strength label and what information was missing — so a claim in the draft can be traced back to the line you supplied, or shown to have no line behind it. The campaign's execution page shows the draft next to its review report, and under 'Why it scored what it scored' you can read what the simulated reader understood, where they stopped, their biggest doubt and what they suggested changing. That reader is an AI simulation that never saw the brief — not a human reviewer — which is exactly why the critique is published in specifics instead of a verdict: you read the reasoning and decide whether it is right about your email.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: The notes the pilot asks for — the phrases you would keep or rewrite, the factual errors, the time you spent editing — are measurements only you can take, because you are the one who still checks the facts, the links and the voice before anything leaves.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: I was asked for feedback and I have nothing to say yet, because I have not run anything through it on something that matters.
alternative_arguments.status_quo: The account sits unused, and the notes they were asked for stay unwritten because there is nothing to write them about.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: After a run produces a draft, you can compare its claims against the compiled knowledge and against the original material you supplied — which turns 'is this true about my product' from a memory test into a side-by-side check. You are still the last check on facts, links and brand voice before anything is copied into your sending tool, which is why the edit you make is the measurement: the pilot asks for one real offer and the phrases you would keep or rewrite, the factual errors, and the time spent editing.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: giving feedback is a favour on top of my own work. After: the feedback is the by-product of checking one real draft against my own material, which I would have to do anyway before sending it.
must_not_say: no claim that editing is faster than writing from scratch, and no editing-time figure — no baseline exists
no aggregate feedback claims ('most testers said...') — no such reports are established
no price, trial or continuation terms
do not imply the notes buy them anything, a discount or future access
alternative_arguments.objection: If the editing takes longer than writing it myself, I have lost the evening and owe an awkward answer.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Sign in, run one real offer, then compare the draft's claims against your own material and note what you kept, what you rewrote and how long it took.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether the editing this draft needs is work they would do again for the rest of the sequence.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: In the workspace they can open a completed run's draft and compare its claims with the compiled knowledge and the original source material they supplied, which is the check the pilot's questions are about.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: It does not establish how long editing takes in general, does not verify their links or voice for them, and does not answer what happens after the pilot.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead on the fact that their edit is the measurement — specific, bounded, and obviously theirs to make.

emails.belief_shift: Before: a machine's opinion of a machine's email is worth nothing, and I would have to take the output on faith. After: the output comes with its sources and its reasoning exposed, so I can check the facts against my own material and judge the critique on whether it is right — which is a different thing from being asked to believe a score.
must_not_say: do not imply the cold reader is a human, a real customer, a focus group or a measurement of anything
no claim that the review predicts or improves opens, clicks, replies, revenue or conversions
no price, plan, trial, discount or free-entry terms
no testimonials, customer names or implied adoption by anyone else
do not promise the compiled facts are complete or correct, or that the draft contains no errors — the reader is still the last check on facts, links and brand voice
do not assume they already ran a campaign, nor that they did not; write so both readers can act
do not assume their tools, list size, revenue, staffing, past email results or urgency
no security, retention or confidentiality reassurance about their material
keep competitor research, the audience map and LinkedIn out of this email
nothing from the older orqAgent agent builder
do not claim the two pages save time or shorten review — no such measurement exists
emails.objection: An AI telling me another AI's email is good proves nothing — nobody has measured whether a human opens it.
emails.tone: Plainer and more technical than the first email; candid about what the review is not, confident about what you can actually read on the page.
emails.call_to_action: Sign in and open your brand's Knowledge page and the review report for your run — or, if you have not run one yet, add the material for one real offer and request one email so there is something to read.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether they trust the draft enough to put their own name on it — decided by reading the facts it was allowed to claim and the reader's stated doubts, rather than by trusting the tool.
emails.next_step_value: In their workspace, the brand's Knowledge page shows the compiled facts with supporting source quotations, evidence identifiers, strength labels and what was missing; a completed campaign's execution page shows the draft alongside the review report, including what the simulated reader understood, where they stopped, their biggest doubt and suggested changes.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing in opens the workspace, not a report: if no campaign has been run, there is no draft or review to open yet. The report is one simulated reader's reading, not a measurement of how real recipients behave, and it does not establish what the product costs after the pilot.
emails.subject_strategy: Concede the suspicion in the subject and point at what is actually readable — the sources behind each claim, and where the cold reader stopped. Curiosity about the working, not a claim about quality.
must_not_reuse: Before anything gets written, your material is compiled into a set of facts the writing is allowed to claim — and then every draft is read by a reader who has never seen the brief, and rewritten where it did not land; that is the part you cannot get from a blank prompt, and it only starts once you put one real offer in.

brief.voice_notes: Brand register: direct and explanatory, careful and almost legalistic about what is not claimed, no hype adjectives; short declarative openers mixed with longer clause-stacked sentences, em dashes and colons to qualify rather than a new sentence. Use the company's own words where they fit: cold read, Knowledge page, execution page, 'Why it scored what it scored', compiled knowledge, source material, reviewed draft. Second person to the reader is fine — this is a request to a specific person with an account — but no first-person named human, no invented founder anecdote and no signature block, since none is captured. Never write a sentence that could describe any AI writing tool; if a paragraph would survive a find-and-replace of the product name, it is the wrong paragraph.

reasons: No persisted market recommendation applies to this campaign.
